analysis.one_liner: Opens federal lands to oil and gas drilling, revives the Keystone pipeline, and tightens oversight of energy futures trading.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with zero cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced amid rising energy prices in late 2021, this bill would have required the Interior Department to immediately resume selling oil and gas leases on federal land and barred the President from pausing or delaying those sales without Congress's approval. It would have authorized the Keystone pipeline's border crossing in Montana without a presidential permit, increased the share of Gulf of Mexico offshore drilling revenue sent to states and coastal communities, and stated the Senate's support for sanctioning the Nord Stream 2 pipeline and withdrawing from the Paris Climate Agreement. It also contained a set of financial-market provisions: new reporting rules for index traders and swap dealers in energy futures, public disclosure of passive index-fund positions, a study of international energy trading rules, and at least 50 new enforcement staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers gain access to more federal leases with fewer delays, and the Keystone pipeline sponsor gets a congressionally granted border crossing free of presidential permitting. Gulf Coast oil-producing states and coastal communities get a larger share of offshore drilling revenue, exempted from automatic budget cuts. Energy futures markets would face more public reporting and enforcement, which backers framed as protection for consumers against price manipulation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas producers and Gulf states

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Secretary to immediately resume federal oil and gas lease sales and prohibits the President from pausing, canceling, or delaying federal leasing without Congressional approval.
Authorizes the TransCanada Keystone pipeline to build and operate its border-crossing facilities in Phillips County, Montana, and eliminates the requirement for a presidential permit.

Directs the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to issue reporting rules for index traders and swap dealers in energy markets, publish monthly data on passive index-fund positions, study international energy futures regulation, and hire at least 50 additional oversight and enforcement employees.
Increases the share of Gulf of Mexico offshore oil and gas revenue distributed to states and coastal communities and exempts those payments from sequestration cuts.

Expresses the Senate's view that the federal government should sanction Nord Stream 2 participants, withdraw from the Paris Climate Agreement, and allow oil and gas leases in the Gulf of Mexico and other federal areas.

analysis.who_pays: Expanded federal leasing and the Keystone authorization would increase extraction of publicly owned oil and gas, with the resulting greenhouse gas emissions borne by the public. Redirecting a larger share of offshore revenue to Gulf states, and shielding those payments from sequestration, reduces money available to the federal Treasury. Much of the bill's declared agenda (Paris withdrawal, Nord Stream 2 sanctions) appears only as a non-binding 'sense of the Senate' with no legal force.

drawbacks.text: Requiring immediate federal lease sales and reviving the Keystone pipeline would increase U.S. oil and gas development and the greenhouse gas emissions that come with it, cutting against the climate goals the same Congress was debating; oil prices are set on global markets, so more domestic leasing does not reliably lower what households pay.

The bill shifts a larger share of Gulf of Mexico offshore revenue to states and exempts those payments from sequestration, reducing federal receipts, and its core 'sense of the Senate' provisions impose no binding change on the administration.
The Keystone provision was largely moot by introduction: the developer had already cancelled the project in June 2021, so a congressional authorization could not by itself revive it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's most genuinely public-serving pieces are the Commodity Futures Trading Commission transparency and enforcement provisions, which would have shed light on speculation in energy markets. But the bill's centerpiece is expanded federal oil and gas leasing and a revived Keystone authorization, whose price benefits for consumers are uncertain and whose climate and public-lands costs are real. Weighing it honestly: a modest pro-consumer market-transparency package wrapped around a large expansion of fossil fuel development on public land.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Hyde-Smith introduced the bill on December 9, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, the committee that oversees the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
No cosponsors ever signed on, including none from the Senate's 50 Republicans.
The committee took no further action, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo prevailed: no expansion of federal leasing mandates, no Keystone revival, and no shift of Gulf offshore revenue away from the Treasury, which leaves the public's climate position unchanged. The bill's modest energy-market transparency provisions died with it, but its centerpiece would have served producers and the pipeline sponsor, so little was lost by ordinary people.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo on federal leasing

for.name: Cindy Hyde-Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, her first and only action on it; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Debbie Stabenow
against.role: Chair, Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup after its referral; the committee took no action on it.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so its level of support beyond the sponsor was never tested.

industries.note: The bill mandates immediate federal lease sales and bars presidential pauses or delays on leasing, expanding producers' access to publicly owned oil and gas. Its stated consumer benefit is lower energy prices through more supply, but that gain is uncertain while the emissions cost falls on the public.

The bill hands one company a congressionally granted border crossing and removes the presidential-permit requirement, a targeted benefit that persists regardless of public need; the project had already been cancelled by the developer.

industries.industry: Energy futures traders and index funds
industries.note: New routine reporting rules, public monthly disclosure of passive index positions, and at least 50 new CFTC oversight and enforcement staff would raise scrutiny and compliance burdens in energy commodity markets. In this bill, the industry's interest in avoiding disclosure runs against the public's interest in market transparency.

industries.industry: Gulf Coast oil-producing states and coastal communities
industries.note: The bill increases their share of offshore drilling revenue and exempts those payments from automatic budget cuts, meaning more federal drilling revenue stays with a small set of states at the Treasury's expense.
